1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune pretrained language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}.
5	In these decoder-only architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens, and the causal attention mask prevents image tokens from attending to later tokens~\cite{wang2025seeing,pei2025rethinking}.
6	The readout token (the final position before action decoding) is the sole multimodal integration point.
7	How representations at this position differ between trained and reference models, and whether the resulting patterns reflect training or inherited backbone structure, remains unknown.
8	
9	Behavioral studies show that VLAs exhibit visual dominance~\cite{grant2026} and underweight instructions~\cite{haon2025}, but existing representational analyses target single architectures.
10	No prior work tests whether instruction routing mechanisms are consistent across backbone families or decomposes training-associated effects from inherited base-model priors.

tool_args.content:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language or language backbones for robotic action prediction, yet how instruction-related information is represented across trained VLAs remains poorly understood.
We study this question through a cross-architecture representational analysis of OpenVLA, TracVLA, and NORA across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained checkpoints with their corresponding reference models.
Using layer-wise action probes, attention profiling, and counterfactual instruction perturbations, we find that the two tested VLM-to-VLA transitions exhibit pronounced peak-to-exit reductions in action-probe decodability, whereas the tested VLA-to-VLA transition shows only small fluctuations.
Trained action-producing VLAs also show measurable sensitivity to instruction perturbations, while L1 instruction-dominant attention largely pre-exists in the underlying pretrained backbones.
These results provide a cross-architecture characterization of instruction-related representations in action-finetuned VLAs and clarify which observed patterns are training-associated versus inherited from reference models.

\paragraph{$R^2$ action probes.}
To measure how much action-relevant information is linearly decodable at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-D action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
$R^2$ near 1.0 means the layer's representation nearly determines the action; a drop from peak to exit layer indicates that action-relevant information becomes less decodable in later processing.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries to prevent within-trajectory leakage (demo-level splitting reduces $R^2$ from $0.7$--$0.9$ to $0.4$--$0.6$ compared to random splitting, confirming that temporal correlations inflate aggregate estimates).
We characterize $\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$ via both effect size and uncertainty: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ is classified as \emph{substantial} exit collapse, representing $\geq 10\%$ absolute change in explained variance on the $R^2$ scale; the qualitative separation between VLM-to-VLA and other conditions is robust to threshold choice: any threshold in $(0.097, 0.156)$ yields identical grouping (Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
95\% CIs are obtained via Monte Carlo cross-validation with demo-level splitting ($n = 1{,}000$ iterations): the canonical peak layer is fixed from the full-data split to avoid winner's-curse bias, and entire demonstrations are resampled without replacement to respect nested temporal dependencies.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}), confirming that observed effects are not artifacts of MLP probe capacity.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Action probes.}
To quantify how much action-relevant structure is accessible at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-DoF action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
We report probe $R^2$ as a measure of action decodability.
Higher $R^2$ indicates that actions are more accurately predictable from that representation under the probe; it should not be interpreted as evidence that the model causally uses that layer for action generation.
We define $\Delta R^2$ as the difference between the maximum layer-wise $R^2$ and the exit-layer $R^2$, and use $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ as a descriptive threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries to prevent within-trajectory leakage (demo-level splitting reduces $R^2$ from $0.7$--$0.9$ to $0.4$--$0.6$ compared to random splitting, confirming that temporal correlations inflate aggregate estimates).
The qualitative separation between VLM-to-VLA and other conditions is robust to threshold choice: any threshold in $(0.097, 0.156)$ yields identical grouping (Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
95\% CIs are obtained via Monte Carlo cross-validation with demo-level splitting ($n = 1{,}000$ iterations): the canonical peak layer is fixed from the full-data split to avoid winner's-curse bias, and entire demonstrations are resampled without replacement to respect nested temporal dependencies.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}), confirming that observed effects are not artifacts of MLP probe capacity.

Taken together, the three analyses separate two empirical patterns.
Peak-to-exit action-probe reductions and counterfactual action sensitivity are most pronounced in trained VLA checkpoints, whereas L1 instruction-dominant attention is already high in the corresponding reference backbones.
Substantial peak-to-exit reductions appear in all tested VLM-to-VLA cells and remain small in the tested VLA-to-VLA cells.
This separation motivates the Discussion, where we distinguish directly supported observations from stronger causal interpretations that require matched training-stage controls.

\subsection{Instruction Sensitivity: Counterfactual Perturbation}
\label{sec:cf_sensitivity}

All trained VLAs exhibit medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity to instruction perturbation (Table~\ref{tab:cf_sensitivity}, Figure~\ref{fig:counterfactual_bar}).

\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.48\columnwidth}
\vspace{-12pt}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.46\columnwidth]{figures/fig_counterfactual_bar.pdf}
\caption{Counterfactual sensitivity (top perturbation condition per cell). Cohen's $d$ for OpenVLA/TracVLA; cosine distance for NORA/reference VLMs.}
\label{fig:counterfactual_bar}
\vspace{-10pt}
\end{wrapfigure}
Across eight cells where Cohen's $d$ is applicable (OpenVLA and TracVLA, four suites each), every perturbation condition yields $d = 0.45$--$1.52$ (Table~\ref{tab:counterfactual_main}).
The ``empty'' condition ranks first in 6 of 8 cells ($d = 1.17$--$1.52$); ``paraphrased'' ranks last in 7 of 8, indicating that VLAs encode instruction content beyond token-level matching.
TracVLA produces systematically higher effect sizes ($d = 0.97$--$1.52$) than OpenVLA ($0.45$--$1.21$).
NORA uses cosine distance (saturated at $1.0$ on Goal; peak $0.275$ on Spatial).
Metric incomparability between trained (Cohen's $d$) and reference (cosine distance) conditions precludes cross-metric amplification ratios (see Appendix~\ref{sec:cf_details_appendix} for metric discussion).

Two OpenVLA cells permit same-metric trained/reference comparison, since the OXE-pretrained baseline also produces actions.
On Spatial, training increases sensitivity across all four conditions ($+0.05$ to $+0.24$), consistent with the small $\Delta R^2 = 0.037$ (below the $0.10$ threshold).
On Long-Horizon, the pattern inverts: the OXE-pretrained model ($d = 1.05$) exceeds the LIBERO-trained model ($d = 0.57$), consistent with small collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.033$) and the general-purpose model maintaining broader instruction responsiveness.

\paragraph{Probing limitations.}
Linear and MLP probes measure decodability, not whether the model causally uses the decoded information for action generation.

64	\paragraph{L1 attention gradient.}
65	At L1, three conditions form a gradient of instruction attention: randomly initialized networks allocate 0/32 instruction-dominant heads ($11.7\%$ text attention, $1.5\times$ text-to-image ratio), Llama-2 base~\cite{touvron2023_llama2} allocates 9/32 ($36.5\%$), and VLA-trained allocates 24/32 ($57.7\%$, $38.2\times$ text-to-image ratio; \S\ref{sec:attention_decomp}).
